summary: One of two FYI documents of commonly asked questions and answers, written by the IETF User Services Working Group, this one aimed at experienced Internet users. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a list of questions that people who already know the basics often ask, with answers.

questions: common questions from experienced internet users
fyi on questions and answers experienced
subtitle: Common questions and answers from experienced Internet users covering infrastructure, DNS, and protocols.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, experienced users repeatedly asked similar questions about infrastructure, protocols, and operations on mailing lists, creating redundant discussions.
tldr.mechanism: The User Services Working Group collected commonly asked questions and answers from major mailing lists, organized them by topic, and published them in this FYI (For Your Information) document as a reference for network operations staff and experienced users.
tldr.outcome: This document codified Internet operational lore, providing practical answers to real-world questions from people actually running networks, reducing repeated discussions on mailing lists.

today: RFC 1207 is Informational and remains a historical record of Internet operational concerns in early 1991. While specific technical issues mentioned (like BIND bugs and SNMP authentication status) are now outdated, the document illustrates what experienced operators cared about as the Internet was transitioning from research infrastructure to broader academic and commercial use. The companion document FYI 4 (RFC 1206) addressed new users' questions, and these two documents together captured the state of Internet knowledge in early 1991.

sections.title: Purpose and Organization
sections.content:
This document is one of two FYI (For Your Information) documents published by the IETF User Services Working Group presenting commonly asked questions and answers from the Internet community. While the companion document (FYI 4) addresses questions from new Internet users, this document targets experienced Internet users—people who already understand the basics and face more advanced operational and technical challenges. The questions and answers are collected from various Internet mailing lists, where network operations staff, system administrators, and advanced users discuss technical issues.

The questions are presented loosely grouped by related topics for easy reading and reference. The answers come directly from mailing list discussions, though some have been abridged for clarity or expanded with additional information to make them more complete. The FYI is designed to be updated as the Internet evolves, with temporal errors corrected in new releases. The document includes pointers to the Q&A mailing lists (quail@ftp.com for discussion, quail-box@ftp.com for submissions) where the community can contribute new questions and answers.
sections.eli5: Experienced Internet people kept asking the same technical questions on email lists. Someone collected all those questions and answers and published them so network managers could find the answers without asking the mailing list again.

sections.title: Internet Infrastructure and Connectivity
sections.content:
The document addresses several questions about the Internet's core infrastructure. One question concerns traffic statistics for the NSFNET (National Science Foundation Network), directing administrators to the Merit/NSFNET Information Services system at nis.nsf.net for statistical data on packet counts and byte counts by type of use (ftp, smtp, telnet, etc.). Another section covers interconnections with non-Internet networks, particularly BITNET and EARN, explaining how these networks use different protocols (IBM RSCS/NJE instead of TCP/IP) but can exchange email through gateways running SMTP.

The document explains that BITNET (in the US) and EARN (in Europe) are cooperating academic networks that support electronic mail, file transfer, and interactive messages. It notes that BITNET and CSNET merged on October 1, 1990, to form CREN. For users who need to reach BITNET nodes, the document provides the addressing format: user%nodename.bitnet@uicvm.uic.edu. This practical guidance helps administrators understand how to bridge between the Internet and these parallel academic networks.
sections.eli5: The document explains how to find statistics about network traffic, and how to send email to people on BITNET and EARN, which were separate academic networks that used different rules than the Internet.

sections.title: Domain Name System Questions and Issues
sections.content:
A substantial section covers DNS (Domain Name System) questions from experienced administrators. One question addresses how to query DNS directly to verify name resolution and understand how short names are expanded at the user's site. The document recommends using tools like dig or nslookup to query DNS directly, allowing administrators to understand how the system resolves names before relying on a central query service. This is practical guidance for debugging naming issues without depending on external services.

The document also addresses technical issues with DNS implementations, particularly BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain, a popular DNS server). It notes that BIND has had problems with polluting its own database, that older versions had severe issues with TCP connections and names with short TTLs (Time To Live), and that upgrading to recent versions often resolves problems. The document also addresses quirks in IBM's DNS implementation and recommends avoiding the combination of old BIND and old IBM servers. Additionally, it covers the proper use of glue records in the DNS zone file and explains DNS case handling, clarifying practical implementation details that administrators encounter.
sections.eli5: The document explains how to use DNS tools to debug name resolution, warns about bugs in old DNS software, and gives practical tips for running DNS servers correctly.

sections.title: Network Management and Protocol Implementation
sections.content:
The document addresses questions about SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), which is used to manage network devices. It mentions that the IETF working group on authentication of SNMP PDUs (Protocol Data Units) was close to a solution as of early 1991, with solid implementations expected by October 1991. The document also advises that before submitting a Management Information Base (MIB)—a data structure describing managed objects—administrators should validate it using tools like MOSY. It directs them to mib-checker@isi.edu for official review and to the /share/ftp/mib directory on venera.isi.edu for installation.

Another section covers SLIP (Serial Line Internet Protocol) and PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol). The document clarifies that SLIP is designed for asynchronous serial lines, not synchronous ones—the opposite of what some thought. It recommends that new implementations should use PPP instead, as PPP works on both sync and async lines and was designed to be useful for many protocols beyond just IP. The document also notes that PPP can be useful in fields beyond Internet communications, such as telecontrol and telemetering, where proprietary incompatible protocols had created maintenance problems.
sections.eli5: The document explains how to validate network management data structures (MIBs), notes that SNMP authentication was being worked on, and clarifies that PPP is better than SLIP for connecting computers over phone lines or serial connections.

sections.title: Practical Operational Guidance
sections.content:
The document provides practical answers to implementation-specific questions. For example, it addresses how to determine whether an OCTET STRING in SNMP output should be displayed as text or as hexadecimal bytes. The answer explains that there is no automatic way to determine this without knowing the specific object, but suggests scanning the octets: if all octets are printable ASCII, display as text; if any are non-printable, display all in hexadecimal notation. The document lists objects marked as DisplayString in MIB-II and notes that these can safely be printed as strings.

Additional guidance covers action-type MIB variables (objects that trigger operations like device reset), the proper structure for describing SNMP actions, and how to implement private MIB objects. Throughout, the document emphasizes that the answers are based on real-world experience from people operating networks and solving problems as they arise. The answers reflect practical solutions that have worked rather than purely theoretical guidance, making the document valuable for operators facing similar situations.
sections.eli5: The document gives practical tips for solving real problems that network administrators face, like how to display certain kinds of data correctly and how to set up network management controls.

sections.title: Reference and Community Process
sections.content:
The RFC includes a comprehensive reference section pointing to related RFCs and resources. References cover DNS specifications (RFC 1034, 1035), SNMP RFCs, SLIP specifications, and other standards. The document emphasizes that it is a living reference: as the Internet evolves and technology changes, the FYI is updated to correct temporal errors and add new questions. The editorial process involves the User Services Working Group and the Q&A mailing lists (quail@ftp.com and quail-box@ftp.com).

The document was created through community contribution, with questions and answers collected from major Internet mailing lists by people who were actively monitoring discussions. The editors acknowledge contributors from academia, commercial organizations (FTP Software Inc., Performance Systems International), and government (ISI, SRI, EDUCOM, Merit). This document represents the collective knowledge of experienced Internet users at a specific moment in time—early 1991—providing a snapshot of the operational practices and common problems that were significant to the Internet community as it scaled beyond academic institutions.
sections.eli5: This RFC is a snapshot of what Internet operators knew and cared about in 1991, collected from their real experiences running networks. It's updated as things change, and people can submit new questions to add to it.
